# Building and publishing a nimble package

Useful code has a bad habit: it gets copied. The first copy still matches the original, the tenth
differs in five places, and nobody knows which one is right. A package is how Nim breaks that habit:
one directory, one version number, one place to fetch the newest code from.

::: {.callout-note}
## What you will be able to do

After this chapter you can lay out a package, write its `.nimble` file, use `nimble check` and
`nimble test`, pick versions with semantic versioning, and publish a package to a Git repository.
:::

## One package, one directory

A nimble package is a directory with a `<name>.nimble` file at its root. The rest follows a shared
convention:

```{.txt}
textstats/
  textstats.nimble
  README.md
  src/
    textstats.nim
  tests/
    test_textstats.nim
```

`src/textstats.nim` is the front door. A user writes `import textstats` and the compiler looks for
that file. Extra modules go in `src/textstats/` and are imported as `import textstats/utils`; a
`private/` directory marks internal modules. That is a convention, not a barrier: the compiler can
still import them when the path is on the search path. `tests/` holds tests, `README.md` a short usage note.

`nimble init` creates this skeleton:

```{.bash}
nimble init textstats
```

The wizard asks for the package type (library, binary, hybrid), version, description, license, and
lowest supported Nim version. It then writes `textstats.nimble`, `src/textstats.nim`,
`src/textstats/submodule.nim`, `tests/test1.nim`, and `tests/config.nims`. Delete what you do not
need; only the `.nimble` file and the code in `src/` are required.

## What goes in the `.nimble` file

The `.nimble` file is Nim code that nimble runs while reading the package. Its basic shape:

```{.ini}
# Package

version       = "0.1.0"
author        = "Sari Dewi"
description   = "Count words and build titles"
license       = "MIT"
srcDir        = "src"


# Dependencies

requires "nim >= 2.0.0"
```

| Line | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `version` | the package version, used by nimble to pick a compatible release |
| `author` | the maintainer name, shown in the package list |
| `description` | a one-line summary of the package |
| `license` | an SPDX identifier, such as `MIT` |
| `srcDir` | the directory holding the code; required when it is not next to the `.nimble` file |
| `requires` | dependencies, including the lowest supported Nim version |

`requires` accepts version ranges: `>=`, `<`, `==`, `^=` for the latest compatible release under
semver, and `~=` for updates within the same minor. So `requires "nim ^= 2.0.0"` means Nim 2.0.0 up
to but excluding 3.0.0, while `requires "nim ~= 2.0.0"` means Nim 2.0.0 up to but excluding 2.1.0. This book needs only the lowest Nim version.

A `.nimble` file may also declare `task` entries, for example one that builds documentation:

```{.ini}
task docs, "Build the documentation":
  exec "nim doc --outdir:docs src/textstats.nim"
```

That task runs with `nimble docs`; `nimble tasks` lists them all.

## A library module and its user

Code that deserves to be a package is used without knowing what is inside. Below are a small module
and a program that uses it. Inside a package the first file lives at `src/textstats.nim`.

```{.nim}
## A tiny reusable module: the kind of code that belongs in a package.

import std/strutils

proc wordCount*(text: string): int =
  ## Count the words in `text`.
  text.splitWhitespace().len

proc titleCase*(text: string): string =
  ## Capitalize the first letter of every word.
  for word in text.splitWhitespace():
    if result.len > 0:
      result.add ' '
    result.add word[0].toUpperAscii & word[1 .. ^1].toLowerAscii

when isMainModule:
  echo wordCount("nim is a small language")
  echo titleCase("nim is a small language")
```

```{.txt}
5
Nim Is A Small Language
```

The star in `wordCount*` exports that procedure; without it the procedure stays private to its
module. `when isMainModule` runs only when the file is compiled as the main program, so one file
serves as both library and runnable example, and importing it prints nothing.

The user needs one import:

```{.nim}
import a01_textstats

echo wordCount("hello brave new world")
echo titleCase("hello brave new world")
```

```{.txt}
4
Hello Brave New World
```

Inside the package that file lives at `src/textstats.nim` and the import is `import textstats`; the
example is named `a01_textstats.nim` and the import follows it. The module name follows the file
name. If an import clashes, add an alias:

```{.nim}
import a01_textstats as ts

echo ts.wordCount("packages are just boxes")
echo ts.titleCase("packages are just boxes")
```

```{.txt}
4
Packages Are Just Boxes
```

A wrong module name fails at compile time, not at runtime:

```{.nim}
import textstats_helpers
```

```{.txt}
main.nim(1, 8) Error: cannot open file: textstats_helpers
```

`main.nim` is the file, `(1, 8)` is line 1 column 8, the start of the module name. `cannot open file`
means the compiler walked its module search path, starting from the calling file's directory, and
found no `textstats_helpers.nim`.

## Day-to-day nimble commands

Two commands carry most of the work while developing:

```{.bash}
nimble check
nimble test
```

`nimble check` validates the package structure. `nimble test` compiles and runs every file in
`tests/` whose name begins with `t`; when everything passes, the last line reads
`Success: All tests passed`.

A binary package declares `bin` in its `.nimble` file; then `nimble build` produces the binary and
`nimble run` builds and runs it. A library has no binary, so `nimble build` stops with
`Nothing to build`; use `nimble check` and `nimble test` instead. `nimble c` compiles a single file.

The install command:

```{.bash}
nimble install
```

With no package name, `nimble install` installs the package in the working directory into `~/.nimble`,
handy for testing before publication. Once published, a user writes `nimble install textstats`. A
package missing from the official list still installs straight from its Git repository URL.

## Versions: major, minor, patch

A version number is not decoration: users rely on it to decide when updating is safe, and nimble to
pick a release. The standard rule, semantic versioning (*semver*), reads `0.1.0` as
`major.minor.patch`:

| Digit | Bumped when |
|---|---|
| `patch` | a bug is fixed without changing how the code is used |
| `minor` | a capability is added and stays compatible |
| `major` | something changes that breaks user code |

Below `1.0.0` any minor release may break compatibility, so users should pin a narrow range such as
`requires "textstats >= 0.1.0 & < 0.2.0"`. From `1.0.0` on the promise is stronger: a breaking change
must bump the major number.

## Publishing to a Git repository

Nimble stores no package code, only a list of names and repository URLs. So the code must be in Git
first:

```{.bash}
git init
git add .
git commit -m "textstats 0.1.0"
git remote add origin git@github.com:sari/textstats.git
git push -u origin main
```

Once the repository exists, the package is registered once; every later release is marked with a tag:

```{.bash}
git tag v0.2.0
git push origin main --tags
nimble publish
```

Nimble reads version-shaped tags such as `v0.2.0` to learn which releases exist, so bump `version`,
commit, then tag. `nimble publish` needs a GitHub account and a personal access token and proposes
the package to the official list in `nim-lang/packages`. Once per package, not per release.

## When a package is ready to be published

Not all code needs to be a package. If only one program uses it, keep it as a module in that project.
A package earns its keep when:

- the same code is used by two projects or more;
- `README.md` shows how to use it: install, import, call;
- tests pass with `nimble test`, so users dare to update;
- the license is explicit, or nobody else may use it;
- the name is not already taken by another package in the official list.

`0.1.0` is fine for a young package: publishing early and fixing fast beats waiting for "perfect",
because mistakes only show up once someone uses the code.

## Exercises

Answers are in [Appendix A](../appendix/answers.qmd).

1. Name four things that must be in place before a package is ready to be published.
2. Without running it, predict the output:
   ```{.nim}
   import a01_textstats as ts

   echo ts.titleCase("NIM DOES NOT CARE")
   ```
3. Lay out a package named `notes`: one module at `src/notes.nim`, one test file in `tests/`, and
   `notes.nimble`. Write out the contents of `notes.nimble`.
4. The code below fails to compile. Fix it, then explain the message:
   ```{.nim}
   import notes_helpers

   echo "loaded"
   ```
5. Pick the next version for these changes: (a) adding a new procedure, (b) fixing a typo in an
   error message, (c) renaming a procedure users already call.

## Summary

- A nimble package is a directory with `<name>.nimble` at the root, code in `src/`, tests in `tests/`.
- The `.nimble` file holds `version`, `author`, `description`, `license`, `srcDir`, and `requires`.
- A procedure used from outside must be exported with `*`; `when isMainModule` separates the demo
  from the library.
- `nimble check` and `nimble test` carry development; `nimble build` is for packages that have a
  binary.
- Semantic versioning tells users when updating is safe; releases are marked with Git tags, and
  `nimble publish` runs once per package.
